title: Conservative sample size planning for population proportion
scenario_markdown: A political polling organization is designing a statewide voter survey. With no prior survey data or historical benchmark available, the research director adopts a conservative planning assumption ($p^* = 0.50$) to guarantee that a $90\%$ confidence interval has a margin of error no greater than $E = 0.04$ ($4.0$ percentage points). Determine the minimum sample size $n$ required.
assumptions: No reliable prior estimate of the true proportion exists, justifying the conservative baseline p* = 0.50
Independent random sampling of registered voters from a large electorate
Normal approximation is valid for large-sample proportion inference
Sample size must always be rounded up to the nearest integer (ceiling function) to prevent exceeding the maximum allowable margin of error
source_refs: Course Module 4: Sampling Distribution & Confidence Interval

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: p* = 0.50, E = 0.04, CL = 0.90. Z* = 1.6448536. Exact continuous n = (1.6448536^2 * 0.25) / 0.0016 = 422.741. Ceiling n = 423. With prior p = 0.20, n = 271, saving 152 respondents. Excel: =ROUNDUP((NORM.S.INV(0.95)^2)*0.25/(0.04^2), 0).

stages.prompt_markdown: Why is $p^* = 0.50$ chosen as the planning value when no preliminary estimate of the proportion is available?

options.text_markdown: The variance function $p(1-p)$ attains its maximum at $p = 0.50$, guaranteeing that the required sample size is large enough for any possible true parameter value.
Because researchers assume voters always split exactly $50/50$ in democratic elections.
options.hint_markdown: Using $p^* = 0.50$ is a mathematical worst-case variance safeguard, not an empirical prediction of an exact tie.

options.text_markdown: Setting $p = 0.50$ minimizes the required sample size and reduces data collection expense.
options.hint_markdown: Setting $p = 0.50$ maximizes $p(1-p) = 0.25$, which yields the maximum possible sample size, not the minimum.

stages.explanation_markdown: The parabola $f(p) = p(1-p)$ reaches its global maximum of $0.25$ at $p = 0.50$. Because sample size is directly proportional to $p(1-p)$, using $p^* = 0.50$ provides a conservative upper bound on the necessary sample size, ensuring that the actual margin of error will be $\le 0.04$ regardless of what the true unknown proportion turns out to be.

stages.prompt_markdown: Using $90\%$ confidence critical value $Z^* = 1.645$, calculate the minimum integer sample size $n = \left\lceil \frac{(Z^*)^2 p^*(1-p^*)}{E^2} \right\rceil$.

options.hint_markdown: Rounding down to $n = 422$ yields a margin of error slightly greater than $0.0400$, violating the strict threshold. Sample sizes must always be rounded up.
The problem specifies a $90\%$ confidence interval ($Z^* = 1.645$), not $95\%$ ($Z^* = 1.960$).

stages.explanation_markdown: For a $90\%$ confidence level, $\alpha = 0.10$ and $Z_{0.05} = 1.64485$ (approx $1.645$). Continuous bound: $n = \frac{(1.6448536)^2 \times (0.50)(0.50)}{(0.04)^2} = \frac{2.70554 \times 0.25}{0.0016} = \frac{0.676386}{0.0016} \approx 422.741$. Taking the ceiling yields $n = 423$. Excel formula: `=ROUNDUP((NORM.S.INV(0.95)^2)*0.25/(0.04^2), 0)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: Suppose a reliable pilot study reveals that the proportion is approximately $p \approx 0.20$. How many fewer respondents would need to be surveyed compared to the conservative baseline of $423$?

options.hint_markdown: Sample size scales with the variance $p(1-p) = 0.20 \times 0.80 = 0.16$, not linearly with $p$.

options.text_markdown: No change: conservative $n = 423$ must always be used regardless of prior knowledge.
options.hint_markdown: When reliable prior information or pilot data exists, using the tighter estimate $p(1-p)$ legitimately reduces sample size requirements.

stages.explanation_markdown: With $p = 0.20$, the variance factor is $p(1-p) = 0.20(0.80) = 0.1600$. The required sample size becomes $n = \left\lceil \frac{2.70554 \times 0.16}{0.0016} \right\rceil = \lceil 270.55 \rceil = 271$. Compared to $423$, the organization saves $423 - 271 = 152$ survey interviews ($35.9\%$ cost reduction) because extreme proportions have much less sampling variability than split ($0.50$) populations.
